newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China approves six Taiwan firms for straits - radio.
newsitem.headline: China approves six Taiwan firms for straits - radio.

text.p: Mainland China on Thursday issued permits to six Taiwan shipping firms allowing them to sail directly across the Taiwan strait for the first time since 1949, Taiwan state radio said.
Taiwan's Uniglory Marine Corp was among the six Taiwan companies to be approved, Uniglory vice president Wang Rong-hsiung told Reuters by telephone.

"They (Beijing) notified us today that we should pick up the licence," Wang said. "We are asking our local agent to contact mainland officials to make the arrangements. We don't have the document right now and are not sure where to pick it up."
Spokesman M.S. Tsay at Taiwan's Yangming Marine Transport Corp said Yangming too had been notified by Beijing that it was among the six approved companies.
Taiwan state radio said a state-sanctioned shipping organisation in Beijing had made telephone contact on Thursday with the private Taiwan Strait Shipping Assocation informing it of the approvals.
Association secretary general Hsu Horng-lieh, reached by telephone, confirmed that he had received notification from Beijing that six Taiwan shipping firms were approved.
Aside from Uniglory and Yangming, Hsu identified them as Wan Hai Lines, Nantai Line, Chinese Maritime Transport Ltd and Kien Hung Shipping.

The approvals came on what Taiwan shipping companies said was the final possible day under mainland law mandating that China's central government approve or reject such applications within 45 days of receiving them.

Beijing's move reciprocates for Taiwan's April approval of five mainland shipping firms to sail long-forbidden routes between Taiwan's southern port of Kaohsiung and China's Fujian province ports of Xiamen and Fuzhou.

Official at Kaohsiung port said on Thursday they expected the first actual crossing could come as early as Friday but had not yet received obligatory notification from any of the five mainland vessels approved by Taiwan.
Such notifications must be filed 24 hours in advance of a ship's arrival, Kaohsiung officials said by telephone.
"If they file by later today, they could still enter our port tomorrow (Friday)," an official said on Thursday morning.
Such crossings would be the first direct sailings between Nationalist-ruled Taiwan and the communist mainland since a civil war split them in 1949.

Taiwan, wary of Beijing's intentions, will not permit direct cargo exchanges. Mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs but rather be processed at a new "offshore transshipment centre" for onward passage to third countries.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be put aboard ships planning to cross directly to the mainland.
Taiwan proposed the offshore transshipment scheme in 1995 in a strategy to ensure direct crossings did not undermine the sovereignty of its exiled Republic of China.
Beijing, taking a different tack, says the routes are domestic links between two provinces, one of which, Taiwan, remains under control of a renegade government.
